At a glance

Best months
May to July for seabird islands, August to October for seawatching and rarities, October to March for geese, swans and waders
Regions
Donegal and the northwestConnemara, Mayo and the western seaboardThe midlands loughs and callowsDublin, the east coast and WicklowThe Burren, Clare and the Shannon callowsKerry and the Shannon estuaryCork, Cape Clear and the southwestWexford and the southeast
Itineraries
A Dublin Layover1 dayThe Wexford Weekend3 daysThe Southwest Islands6 daysThe Western Seaboard8 daysIreland End to End11 days
Getting around
A hire car reaches every region on this page. The island is small enough that the far southwest is five hours from the far north, and the border crosses without a stop

When to Go

The Irish birding year has three peaks rather than one. Seabirds fill the cliffs from March to July, migration runs along the coasts through August to October, and the estuaries hold their biggest flocks from November to February.

Spring

March to June

Seabirds come back to the ledges in March, summer migrants arrive through April, and by May every woodland is singing from before five in the morning.

Go for Breeding seabirds, full song, and the longest days of the year in the north.

Trade off Rooms cost the most from Easter onward, and island boats need booking weeks ahead in June.

Typical daily average March 3 to 9 °C / 37 to 48 °F, April 4 to 12 °C / 39 to 54 °F, May 7 to 15 °C / 45 to 59 °F, June 10 to 18 °C / 50 to 64 °F

Autumn

July to October

Wader passage builds from July, the coasts fill with migrants through September, and October is when a rarity can turn up almost anywhere.

Go for Big wader counts, seawatching in an onshore blow, and the best chance of a bird from a long way off course.

Trade off Song has stopped, so birds are identified on plumage and call, and the seabird colonies are empty by August.

Typical daily average July 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F, August 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F, September 10 to 17 °C / 50 to 63 °F, October 8 to 13 °C / 46 to 55 °F

Winter

November to February

Geese, swans and waders pack the estuaries, starlings gather over the reedbeds at dusk, and raptors are easy over open ground.

Go for Six figure goose and wader flocks, murmurations, and reserves you have largely to yourself.

Trade off Daylight is short, and the island boats stop for the winter.

Typical daily average November 5 to 10 °C / 41 to 50 °F, December 3 to 8 °C / 37 to 46 °F, January 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F, February 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F

Itineraries

1 day

A Dublin Layover

Dublin (DUB), Bull Island, Dublin

North Bull Island is a UNESCO biosphere reserve inside the city limits, twenty minutes from the centre by bus. Half a day covers saltmarsh, mudflat and dune.

  1. 1Dublin
  2. 2Wexford
  3. 3Kilmore Quay

3 days

The Wexford Weekend

Dublin (DUB), Wexford, Kilmore Quay

The Slobs for geese in winter, or the Saltees for seabirds in summer. Two very different trips over the same ground depending on the month.

  1. 1Skibbereen
  2. 2Portmagee
  3. 3Dingle

6 days

The Southwest Islands

Cork (ORK), Cape Clear, Kerry, the Skelligs

Built around two boat days, both weather dependent, so leave slack. Cape Clear in autumn for passage, the Skelligs from April for the gannetry.

  1. 1Ennis
  2. 2Clifden
  3. 3Belmullet

8 days

The Western Seaboard

Shannon (SNN), the Burren, Connemara, Mayo, Donegal

A run up the Atlantic coast taking the Burren, the Mullet and the Donegal headlands. Best in late May and June for Corncrake, or September for seawatching.

11 days

Ireland End to End

Dublin (DUB), Wicklow, Wexford, Cork, Kerry, Clare, Connemara, Donegal

The full circuit, anticlockwise, which is how most operators route it. Ten to twelve days gives each region a real morning rather than a drive-through.

Donegal and the northwest

Sea cliffs, machair and wild loughs across Ireland's most northerly county

Donegal takes the full weight of the Atlantic, and its headlands are among the best seawatching in Europe when the wind swings northwest. Inland, the Bluestack and Derryveagh mountains hold breeding waders on blanket bog that has largely gone elsewhere.

Look for: Barnacle Goose, Whooper Swan, Golden Eagle, Red-billed Chough, Peregrine Falcon, Corn Crake

Parks and reserves: Glenveagh National Park, Sheskinmore Nature Reserve, Inch Levels Wildfowl Reserve, Lough Swilly wetlands (reserve)

Stops: , the most northerly point on the Irish mainland, a headland walked from a car park at Banba's Crown, watched for chough, gannets and passing seabirds , a tidal bay near Malin Head reached from the coast road, its mudflats holding wintering brent geese, wigeon and large wader flocks , an NPWS wildfowl reserve on Inch Island crossed by a causeway road, with hides and a looped walk over wet grassland thick with whooper swans and geese , a sea lough watched from the shore road at Rathmullan, where thousands of whooper swans and Greenland white-fronted geese winter on the reclaimed fields , a National Park run by the OPW and NPWS with a shuttle bus from the visitor centre to the castle, where reintroduced golden eagles soar over the glen , an island reached by a booked passenger ferry from Magheroarty pier, one of the last Donegal strongholds of the corn crake and a breeding site for chough , an NPWS nature reserve of dune, lake and marsh between Ardara and the coast, walked on marked paths for chough, corn crake and wintering wildfowl , a sea cliff headland walked from a roadside car park above Dunfanaghy, with chough, guillemots, razorbills and fulmars nesting on the ledges below

Visitor centres: Glenveagh National Park Visitor Centre

Also covers: Letterkenny

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out along the Inishowen coast near Malin Head, and otters and Irish hares forage around Sheskinmore's dune slacks through the year. Basking sharks pass offshore between May and July.

Where to Stay1 place to stay

Connemara, Mayo and the western seaboard

Blanket bog, offshore island and sea loch along the Atlantic coast of Galway and Mayo

Bog, lake and a coastline of islands and inlets. This is where Ireland's remaining Corncrakes hang on, on the machair of the Mullet and the offshore islands, and where the seabird passage past the Mayo headlands is heaviest in autumn.

Look for: Corn Crake, Red-billed Chough, Red Grouse, Merlin, Greater White-fronted Goose, Whooper Swan

Parks and reserves: Connemara National Park, Wild Nephin Ballycroy National Park, Lough Corrib (reserve), Clare Island (island reserve)

Stops: , a National Park of bog, heath and mountain climbed on the waymarked Diamond Hill trail from the visitor centre at Letterfrack, open to all , a National Park of Atlantic blanket bog crossed by a boardwalk trail, begun at the visitor centre in Ballycroy village, open to all , a fishing harbour on the Connemara coast and the departure point for the Inishbofin ferry, open to all with no booking needed to watch from the quay , an inhabited island reached by a forty-five minute ferry from Cleggan, its machair and heath protected as a Special Area of Conservation for corncrake and seals , a small pier south of Louisburgh and the departure point for the Clare Island and Inishturk ferries, open to all , an inhabited island in Clew Bay reached by ferry from Roonagh Quay, its cliffs and heath home to breeding chough and a resident colony of grey seals , a lakeside town on Lough Corrib's western shore with a public pier and boat access onto the lake's islands and reed fringe, open to all , a sheltered estuary and sand island on the Mayo coast, a Special Protection Area watched from the shore road for waders and geese in winter

Visitor centres: Connemara National Park Visitor Centre, Wild Nephin National Park Visitor Centre

Also covers: Louisburgh

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the Stags rocks off Inishbofin and around Clare Island all year, with pups born on quiet beaches in September and October. Otters fish the sheltered inlets of Killala Bay and the shallows of Lough Corrib, most easily seen at first light.

The midlands loughs and callows

Cutover bog, lake and river callows across the central lowlands of Ireland

The Shannon floods its callows every winter and the wet grassland that results carries Whooper Swan and Greenland White-fronted Goose in numbers. The big midland loughs hold diving duck and the reedbeds behind them hold the marsh birds.

Look for: Whooper Swan, Common Snipe, Northern Lapwing, Eurasian Curlew, Greater White-fronted Goose

Parks and reserves: Lough Boora Discovery Park (reserve), Bog of Allen Nature Centre (reserve), Lough Ree (reserve), Lough Ennell (reserve)

Stops: , a former industrial bog restored as a public park with waymarked trails and a sculpture walk, open to all with a car park and cafe , an Irish Peatland Conservation Council reserve and visitor centre at Lullymore, open to the public with a raised bog trail behind the building , a monastic site on an esker above the River Shannon, its surrounding callows and reed marsh viewed from the visitor path, open to all , a shoreline village on Lough Ree's western shore reached by road, its open water and reed fringe watched from the public lakeshore path , a limestone lake north of Mullingar seen from the public road on its shore, wintering white-fronted geese on the surrounding farmland , a Special Protection Area lake south of Mullingar watched from the lakeshore park at Lilliput, open to all with a car park , a ruined tower house above the Little Brosna river's flood callows near Lorrha, a Special Protection Area seen from the surrounding lanes , a stretch of seasonally flooded riverside grassland watched from the road and towpath around Shannonbridge, open access at any time. Whooper Swan flocks in winter and breeding waders

Visitor centres: Lough Boora Discovery Park, Bog of Allen Nature Centre

Also watch for: Otters and Irish hares are regularly seen along the boardwalks of Lough Boora Discovery Park, especially in early morning. The callows flood each winter between November and February, drawing wintering wildfowl onto the wet grassland that surrounds Lough Ree and the Little Brosna river.

Dublin, the east coast and Wicklow

Dublin Bay mudflats, an offshore tern colony and mountain moorland above Glendalough

The easiest birding in Ireland to reach, and better than it has any right to be. Bull Island sits inside the city and takes waders in thousands, and the Wicklow uplands half an hour south hold Red Grouse and Merlin.

Look for: Brant Goose, Roseate Tern, Bar-tailed Godwit, Red Knot, Peregrine Falcon, Whinchat

Parks and reserves: North Bull Island Nature Reserve, Rogerstown Estuary Nature Reserve, Rockabill (reserve), Wicklow Mountains National Park (Glendalough)

Stops: , an NPWS nature reserve and Dublin's first bird sanctuary, reached by a causeway road you can simply drive onto, its mudflats thick with brent geese and wading birds in winter , an NPWS nature reserve and Ramsar wetland viewed from the causeway and shoreline paths near Rush, simply turn up to scan for brent geese and godwits , a tidal estuary crossed by the Malahide viaduct and viewed from footpaths on both shores, simply turn up to watch brent geese and wintering waders , an island tern colony reached only by a booked summer boat trip from Skerries harbour, Europe's largest roseate tern colony crowding the rocks in June and July , a National Park with an NPWS information office at Glendalough you can simply walk into, its open moorland home to peregrine falcon, red grouse and whinchat , a BirdWatch Ireland nature reserve of coastal wetland walked on a boardwalk trail with hides, and a beach nearby warded each summer for breeding little terns , a coastal headland walked on cliff paths from Howth village, simply turn up to watch guillemot, razorbill, kittiwake and peregrine on the sea cliffs , an NPWS nature reserve of tidal mudflat and salt marsh walked from a roadside path near Baldoyle, holding curlew, redshank and brent geese in winter

Visitor centres: Wicklow Mountains National Park Information Office, Glendalough, Dublin Bay Biosphere

Also covers: Ballsbridge, Maynooth

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the sandbanks of Dublin Bay and are often watched from Bull Island's shoreline. Red deer roam the open mountain of Wicklow, most visible during the rut in September and October.

The Burren, Clare and the Shannon callows

Limestone pavement, turlough and Atlantic headland across County Clare, an hour south of Galway

Limestone pavement over a warm sea, with a flora found nowhere else in these islands and the Cliffs of Moher seabird colonies at the western edge. The Shannon callows to the east flood every winter.

Look for: Red-billed Chough, Sooty Shearwater, Manx Shearwater, Great Shearwater, Northern Wheatear, Eurasian Curlew

Parks and reserves: Burren National Park, Dromore Woods and Loughs Nature Reserve, Loop Head (reserve), Portumna Forest Park (reserve)

Stops: , a seawatching headland walked from a small roadside car park at the tip of the Loop Head peninsula, watched every autumn for passing shearwaters and skuas , an OPW lighthouse and signal station open to climb at the tip of the peninsula, with chough and peregrine on the cliffs below , a National Park of limestone pavement, hazel scrub and turlough walked on looped trails from the Mullaghmore car park, open to all , an NPWS nature reserve of oak woodland, fen and turlough walked on looped trails from a car park near Corofin, open year round , a turlough on the southern edge of the Burren seen from the lane along its shore, filling and emptying through the year with the water table , the largest turlough in Ireland, seen from the road that runs along its edge near Craughwell, a roadside stop rather than a managed reserve , a harbour village on Lough Derg's western shore, with a viewing point over the island where a pair of white-tailed eagles first nested wild in Ireland in 2012 , a Coillte forest park on Lough Derg's northern shore, its boardwalk crossing callow grassland on the edge of the Shannon callows, whooper swan in winter

Visitor centres: Loop Head Lighthouse Visitor Experience, Burren National Park

Also covers: Limerick

Also watch for: Spring gentian and dense burnet rose cover the limestone pavement through April and May, alongside most of Ireland's native orchid species. Common dolphins and basking sharks pass close to the Loop Head cliffs between June and September, often seen from the same points used for watching seabirds.

Kerry and the Shannon estuary

Ocean rock stacks, a mountain peninsula and a wide tidal estuary in the southwest

Skellig Michael's gannetry and the Blasket sounds on one side, the vast Shannon estuary mudflats on the other. Kerry also holds the Irish population of Ring Ouzel and some of the last native oakwood.

Look for: Northern Gannet, Atlantic Puffin, Manx Shearwater, White-tailed Eagle, Red-billed Chough

Parks and reserves: Killarney National Park, Great Skellig Nature Reserve (Skellig Michael), Little Skellig Nature Reserve, Puffin Island Nature Reserve, Tralee Bay Nature Reserve

Stops: , a rock island and UNESCO World Heritage site reached by a licensed summer boat trip from Portmagee. Northern Gannet, European Storm Petrel and Atlantic Puffin nesting on the slopes , a National Parks and Wildlife Service reserve island passed close by boat en route to Skellig Michael, no landing allowed. Ireland's largest Northern Gannet colony, tens of thousands of pairs , a National Parks and Wildlife Service reserve island off Bolus Head, passed by boat from Portmagee with no landing. Large colonies of Atlantic Puffin, Manx Shearwater and storm petrel , a cliff road and headland walked from the roadside viewing points, open access at any time. Red-billed Chough on the grassy slopes and seabirds passing below the cliffs , a National Park free to enter at any time, with Muckross Lake and its woods walked from the car park. Reintroduced White-tailed Eagle over the lakes and red deer , a National Parks and Wildlife Service reserve of mudflat, saltmarsh and shingle spit, watched from the shore road at any time. Wintering Brant Goose and wader flocks on the tideline , a Kerry County Council eco-tourism centre on reclaimed wetland, open to visitors with a boardwalk and hides to turn up to. Wildfowl and waders on the lagoons beside Tralee Bay

Visitor centres: Killarney House and Gardens Visitor Centre, Tralee Bay Wetlands Centre

Also covers: Portmagee

Also watch for: Grey seals gather on the rocks below Skellig Michael and Puffin Island through the summer, and common dolphins follow the boats out from Portmagee. Red deer rut in Killarney National Park each October, and otters fish the callows of the Shannon in early morning light.

Cork, Cape Clear and the southwest

A chain of Atlantic headlands and an island observatory off Ireland's south coast

Cape Clear is Ireland's Fair Isle: an observatory island at the south-west corner that takes seabird passage in autumn and rarities with it. The Cork harbour mudflats behind it are nationally important for waders.

Look for: Manx Shearwater, Sooty Shearwater, Great Shearwater, European Storm Petrel, Red-billed Chough

Parks and reserves: Cape Clear Island (island reserve), Capel Island and Knockadoon Head Nature Reserve, Mizen Head (reserve), Old Head of Kinsale (reserve), Galley Head (reserve)

Stops: , a bird observatory on an island reached by ferry from Baltimore or Schull, open to visiting birders. Ireland's premier landfall for rare migrants and a seawatching base for shearwaters , a fishing village and the main ferry departure point for Cape Clear and Sherkin Island, simply turn up for the harbour and pier. Gannets and terns fishing in the sound , a headland and former signal station walked from the visitor car park on a cliff path, open to all. A seawatching point for shearwaters and skuas moving west , a narrow headland walked along a public right of way beside the golf course, free to walk at any time. Sooty Shearwater and Great Shearwater pass close in autumn winds , a fishing village and headland walked from the pier, simply turn up at any time. Peregrine hunting over the bay and seabirds passing the cliffs at dawn , a lighthouse headland walked from the roadside car park, open access at any time. A seawatching point looking south over open Atlantic water for shearwaters and petrels , a large natural harbour and estuary watched from several shoreline points around Cobh and Great Island, open access at any time. Wintering wildfowl and wader flocks on the mudflats , a National Parks and Wildlife Service reserve covering an island and headland near Youghal, viewed from the shore at any time. Seabirds and migrant passerines on the headland

Also covers: Youghal

Also watch for: Common dolphins and minke whales are regularly seen from the headlands between July and October, with basking sharks passing Mizen Head and the Old Head of Kinsale in early summer. Grey seals haul out below Galley Head and around Cape Clear all year.

Wexford and the southeast

Estuary slobland and coastal lagoons at Ireland's south-east corner

The Wexford Slobs hold most of the world's Greenland White-fronted Geese every winter, on reclaimed polder beside the harbour. Saltee and the Hook add seabirds and a migration point in the same corner.

Look for: Greater White-fronted Goose, Brant Goose, Roseate Tern, Black-tailed Godwit, Eurasian Whimbrel

Parks and reserves: Wexford Wildfowl Reserve (North Slob), The Raven Nature Reserve, Ballyteigue Burrow Nature Reserve, Saltee Islands (island reserve), Lady's Island Lake (island reserve)

Stops: , a National Parks and Wildlife Service reserve on reclaimed sloblands, open daily and free to walk in with a tower hide. Greenland White-fronted Geese and Brant Geese in winter , a National Parks and Wildlife Service dune and forest reserve at Curracloe, walked from the beach car park. Wintering geese roost in the pines and migrants pass through in autumn , a brackish coastal lagoon and bird sanctuary watched from the causeway and shoreline track, free to visit any time. Common Tern and Roseate Tern nest on the shingle islands , a shallow farmland lagoon watched from the boreen along its northern shore, a well-known autumn site for rare waders blown in from North America , a headland walked out from the lighthouse car park at the tip of the peninsula, simply turn up. A seawatching point for shearwaters and gannets passing close inshore , a privately owned seabird sanctuary reached by a summer boat trip from Kilmore Quay, weather permitting. Puffin, Common Murre and Razorbill nesting on the cliffs of Great Saltee , a low headland and beach walked from the roadside car park near Carne, open access at any time. A migration watchpoint for terns and skuas moving offshore in autumn , a National Parks and Wildlife Service dune and saltmarsh reserve near Kilmore Quay, walked in from the beach car park. Golden Plover and Black-tailed Godwit flocks on the mudflats

Visitor centres: Wexford Wildfowl Reserve Visitor Centre

Also covers: Kilkenny

Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the sandbanks off the Saltee Islands and around Carnsore Point year round, with pups born on the islands in autumn. Irish hares are protected across the North Slob and are easiest to see at dawn in winter, when the wintering geese are also out on the fields.

Birding Community

Irish birding is a small and welcoming world. These are the bodies to know, and two of them run the reserves and the observatory on this page. Find a birding organisation near you in our worldwide directory

Alongside the national bodies below, Ireland has 7 local bird clubs across 5 regions. They run the walks and the counts, and most of them welcome visitors. See every Irish club by region.

BirdWatch Ireland BirdLife in Ireland, and the owner or manager of several reserves on this page including Wexford and Cape Clear. Visit National Parks and Wildlife Service The state agency behind the national parks and nature reserves, and the source for designations and site data. Visit Cape Clear Bird Observatory The observatory at the south-west corner, running since 1959, and where Irish seabird passage is counted. Visit Irish Rare Bird Committee The national records committee, and the reference for what has actually occurred in Ireland. Visit Irish Birding The national sightings service, and how Irish birders find out what has turned up where. Visit

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Ireland?

May and June for breeding seabirds, Corncrake and full song. September and October for seabird passage off the southern and western headlands, which is world class in the right wind. October to March for geese, swans and waders, when Ireland holds internationally important numbers.

Where should I go for a first Irish birding trip?

Wexford in winter or Kerry in summer. The Wexford Slobs put most of the world's Greenland White-fronted Geese within sight of a visitor centre; Kerry gives you the Skelligs gannetry, Chough on every clifftop and the Shannon estuary an hour away.

Do I need a car?

Yes, for everything except Dublin. Bull Island is on a city bus route and Wicklow is reachable by train and taxi, but the west coast, the Burren and the Wexford Slobs all need one, and rural bus services are thin.

Which Irish birds are hard to find in Britain?

Greenland White-fronted Goose in that concentration, and Corncrake, which is effectively gone from Britain outside the Hebrides. Chough is far more widespread here than in England. Ireland also lacks a number of common British birds entirely, including Tawny Owl, Willow Tit and Marsh Tit.

Is Cape Clear worth the journey?

In autumn, in a southwesterly, yes. It is Ireland's seawatching station and the shearwater and skua passage past it can be extraordinary. In flat calm it is a quiet island with a ferry timetable, so watch the forecast before you commit.

Can I land on Skellig Michael?

Only with a licensed boat operator, only between May and September, and only when the sea allows. Landings are capped and book out months ahead. The gannetry on Little Skellig is watched from the water either way, so an eco-tour that circles both is the reliable option.

What about Northern Ireland?

It has a page of its own. Rathlin, Lough Foyle, Strangford and the Mournes are all north of the border, and they sit under a different set of agencies and a different certification scheme, so treating them as Irish regions would be misleading in both directions.

How much does an Irish birding trip cost?

Accommodation is the largest line and the west coast is seasonal, so July and August cost the most by some way. Almost every site on this page is free to walk; the boats are the real expense.

When do the geese and swans arrive?

Greenland White-fronted Geese reach Wexford in October and leave in April. Icelandic Whooper Swans follow the same calendar on the midlands callows. Light-bellied Brent arrive on the east coast from late August.
